Self & Creativity I · Attention

Creativity needs more than one attention style. Open to invent. Focus to finish.

Open-monitoring promotes divergent thinking; focused attention is a different job.

(Tao of Creativity)

U6.1 · Self & Creativity I — Attention

1 · Two jobs, two minds

Divergent work multiplies kinds; convergent work finds the fit. Schedule them apart.

Craft notes that one creative act may hold both divergent and convergent thinking.

(Craft 2000, 30)

Image: Pen drawing of Leonardo's flying machine design.

Leonardo Design for a Flying Machine, c. 1488 · Leonardo da Vinci · Public domain · Source

Bridge to U1/U2. Chen/Guilford framing stays available; keep classroom language simple.

U6.1 · Self & Creativity I — Attention

2 · Open-monitoring vs focused attention

OM notices what arises without fixing; FA returns to one object. They are not the same practice.

OM meditation induces a control state that promotes divergent thinking.

(Colzato, Ozturk, and Hommel 2012, 1)

Image: A page from Beethoven's 1812 sketchbook: hurried ink notation across many staves as themes for the Seventh Symphony are tried out.

Sketches for the second movement of Symphony no. 7, op. 92 (Petter Sketchbook, 1812) · Ludwig van Beethoven (sketchbook); Daderot (photograph, public-domain dedication) · Public domain · Source

Definitions from the study Method. Classroom dose later ≠ 35 min.

U6.1 · Self & Creativity I — Attention

3 · Opening feeds ideation

After open-monitoring, people did better on a divergent task in the lab study.

First, OM meditation induces a control state that promotes divergent thinking.

(Colzato, Ozturk, and Hommel 2012, 1)

Image: Pencil sketchbook page of a landscape from the Lines family sketchbook.

Lines family sketchbook - Disc1 009 · Lines family (19th century) · Public domain · Source

Honest: one small laboratory study. Not a talent claim.

U6.1 · Self & Creativity I — Attention

4 · Focus is not magic selection

Why: the study predicted focused-attention would help convergent thinking — it did not hold up. What then: use FA to return to one object when you already have options; do not expect it to invent the right pick for you.

FA meditation did not sustain convergent thinking as predicted.

(Tao of Creativity — after Colzato et al. 2012)

Image: A Pugh concept-selection spreadsheet: criteria such as reliability and safety with weights in rows, four design concepts scored in columns, and totals at the bottom.

Pugh Concept Selection · Chattons2 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Source

Why/what-then: students must not leave thinking FA = automatic good picks. Convergent work still needs criteria, comparison, and craft — attention style is only one tool.

U6.1 · Self & Creativity I — Attention

5 · Incubation needs partial attention

Walk, shower, craft — leave a problem half-held so new links can surface.

The less you try to direct the process the more creative the conclusions are likely to be.

(Csikszentmihalyi 1996)

Image: Two pages of Orville Wright's diary for 17 December 1903: dense handwriting on squared notebook paper recording that day's series of flight tests.

Wright diary · Orville Wright · Public domain · Source

Personal creativity / incubation chapter language — keep classroom paraphrase short.

U6.1 · Self & Creativity I — Attention

6 · Dose honesty + Opt-out

Opt-out means: you may skip the embodied warm-up — sit quietly or jump to listing — no explanation. Dose honesty means: the lab used ~35 minutes; our classroom version is shorter and untested — never pretend the minutes match.

Adaptation is allowed. Pretending the minutes match is not.

(Tao of Creativity)

Image: Photograph of adults seated around tables in a workshop classroom.

People in workshop class · Harless Todd (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service) · Public domain · Source

Define Opt-out on the slide for teenagers. Lab card repeats it. Consent before technique.

U6.1 · Self & Creativity I — Attention

Recall check

Alone, from memory, 3 minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. Name the two attention modes from the study.
  2. Which mode helped divergent thinking?
  3. Did FA reliably boost convergent scores?
  4. Why schedule open and close apart?
  5. What must every embodied warm-up offer?

Course geometric background · threshold · #7a624a21 · Original course SVG

Answers:

1. Open-monitoring and focused-attention.

2. Open-monitoring (Colzato et al. 2012, 1).

3. No — not significant in that study.

4. Different cognitive jobs; judging early costs originality (U2 bridge).

5. Opt-out.

Lab · Attention practice

Two short exercises. Portfolio traces only — no wellness theatre.

Save warm-up note (or Opt-out mark) and attention brief.

Course geometric background · branching · #e18a0dc7 · Original course SVG

U6.1 · Self & Creativity I — Attention

Exercise 1 · Open-monitoring warm-up

Three minutes of noticing breath and thought without fixing — then 5 minutes of divergent listing on today’s brief. Opt-in means the default is non-participation; opt-out means the default is participation. Here: skip to listing only.

OM meditation induces a control state that promotes divergent thinking.

(Colzato, Ozturk, and Hommel 2012, 1)

Write: Opt-in or Opt-out; then count of idea kinds after listing.

Image: Rodin's bronze The Thinker: a seated nude man leans forward, chin resting on his hand, absorbed in thought before acting.

The Thinker · Auguste Rodin (sculpture); Cleveland Museum of Art (photograph, CC0) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Timer: 3 min warm-up + 5 min listing.
  • Opt-out: sit quietly or jump to listing — no explanation required.
  • Study used ~35 min; this is an untested classroom adaptation.
  • Not the U2 6-3-5 pairing — different operation.

U6.1 · Self & Creativity I — Attention

Exercise 2 · Attention brief

For your live brief: mark when you will open (OM window) and when you will focus (FA window). One sentence each.

Two sentences: open window + focus window for the brief.

Image: Historic plate showing drafting-room layout and method diagrams from 1918.

Drafting room methods (1918) (14591687900) · Charles Dickey Collins · Public domain · Source

  • Timer: 10 minutes.
  • Pair-share once.
